title: 本地 Skill Storage 并发读取复现 HTTP 544
result: Reproduced matching HTTP 544 DatabaseTimeout in two GET bursts at actual peak HTTP concurrency 800; LIST at 800 passed this single burst.

offlineAnalysis.quantileMethod: nearest rank: sorted[ceil(p*n)-1]; may differ from runner summary floor(p*n)

latencyDefinitions.headersMs: client request call through response headers; includes connect, remote processing, and network
latencyDefinitions.responseWaitMs: headers sent through response headers; still includes remote/network wait
latencyDefinitions.bodyDrainMsDerived: max(0, elapsedMs - headersMs); includes drain/validation/hash; already buffered bytes may predate headers return
latencyDefinitions.cpuSingleCoreEquivalentPct: process user+system CPU / wall time * 100; does not prove no short scheduling pauses

established: Both GET C800 runs reached measured peak 800 HTTP in-flight and received actual HTTP 544 DatabaseTimeout responses, with zero client_error categories.
Connector queue was zero for these runs; event-loop p95 delay was below 3 ms and maximum below 118 ms, much smaller than multi-second response waits.
GET C800 timeout bodies were tiny and drained quickly; the dominant measured latency preceded response headers.
The confirmation failure rate denominator is 1175 actual attempts, not 1600 planned requests; 425 requests were not started.
notEstablished: Which internal DatabaseTimeout branch fired: Knex acquire timeout, pg connection timeout, or PostgreSQL 57014 query cancellation.
Whether pool size, slow SQL, DB/service/proxy queuing, storage backend access, or another service-side factor is the root cause.
HTTP in-flight is not the number of occupied DB connections.
The post-header drain measurement alone does not isolate all object transfer time, since data may already be buffered before headers become observable.
Public endpoint results are not a latency-equivalent replay of the Runner private-network path.
limitations: GET C400 and LIST C400 had observed maximum event-loop stalls of about 1.74 s and 1.95 s respectively, so the full ramp cannot be described as completely free of client scheduling effects.
Each run is a bounded burst, not a sustained capacity test.
v1 first run and revised confirmation differ in stop timing; compare actual completed requests and per-request measurements, not planned counts alone.

supports: Under these bounded local/public-path bursts, GET C800 reproduced DatabaseTimeout in two runs; LIST C800 completed all 1600 requests with HTTP 200 and measured peak 800 in-flight.
The failure is workload/path dependent in these observations; the client can issue and finish 1600 LIST requests at the same configured/measured peak without local errors.
The 19 final GETs matched original baseline hashes and all 19 final LISTs succeeded, supporting recovery for these tested objects at low concurrency.
doesNotSupport: LIST success does not prove absence of DB or service queuing: LIST C800 header p95 was about 6.41 seconds.
Cannot conclude that the object download holds a DB connection; ordinary v1.48.9 GET metadata transactions commit before backend getObject.
Cannot attribute GET failures specifically to OSS, SQL, local pool size, PG global capacity, or exact internal DatabaseTimeout branch without server evidence.
Cannot claim C800 is a deterministic failure threshold, nor extrapolate these bursts to sustained throughput/capacity.
The two GET failure percentages are not a controlled trend: stop timing and actual request counts differ; service state and run ordering were not randomized.

Local public-path reproduction confirms this error can occur independently of Agent task orchestration, but does not prove it is the identical internal cause of the earlier Runner private-path failures.
recommendations: Report the GET/LIST contrast and exact actual denominators as a reproduction result, not a root-cause finding.
Correlate the recorded request IDs/timestamps with Storage original errors, SQLSTATE, effective pool settings, and acquire/query timing before changing pool capacity.
Retain LIST high tail latency as an observation even though no request failed; report low-concurrency recovery and verified hashes separately.

limitations: Same HTTP error does not prove the same internal cause as the earlier Runner failure.
Public HTTP path differs from the original private VPC path.
Repeated reads of 19 SKILL.md files and directory listings do not model every file or mixed production workload.
Concurrency is actual outstanding HTTP requests, not QPS, distinct Skills, or SQL connections. Completion rate is not a controlled offered request rate.
Short bursts and two failing GET runs do not establish an exact sustainable capacity limit.
Storage connection count 21 is an observation, not a verified pool-size setting.
2-second GET DB samples and 1-second LIST samples can miss short peaks. GET transaction age was not captured.
LIST idle-in-transaction sample age was short, so state counts alone do not prove a connection leak.
The C400 batches had material local event-loop pauses; do not interpret the whole matrix as a clean capacity benchmark.
No current-run RDS CPU series, Storage pool queues, worker resources, raw exception/SQLSTATE, or S3 timings were captured.

scope.dbObservationMethod: Supabase connector SELECT of pg_stat_activity counts, state/waits, aggregate ages and fixed query classification; no business queries or mutations

observation.maxIntervalReason: A deliberate sampler upgrade between GET and LIST control added last-query class and transaction/state ages; no load window crossed this upgrade.

listControlTransactionClassification.interpretation: Only BEGIN, SET_CONTEXT and SEARCH were observed while idle in transaction. Sampled transaction ages were at most 129 ms and idle-state ages at most 68 ms; these states do not establish long transactions or a connection leak.

cleanup.stopReason: Parent created STOP-DB-OBSERVER; loop exited on sentinel with code 85.

supportedConclusions: The same Storage backend returned DatabaseTimeout HTTP544 in two independent local GET bursts with concurrency 800, without OMA sessions or Sandbox creation.

No sampled global database connection pressure, Storage SQL lock waiting or blocked Storage connection coincided with these bursts. Storage connections reached 21; this is an observed count, not a verified pool configuration limit.
The LIST control at concurrency 800 completed all 1600 requests successfully. The subsequent low-concurrency GET/LIST checks both succeeded on all 19 Skills.
GET and LIST behaved differently at the same configured concurrency, narrowing investigation toward their Storage request paths or per-path resource use, without proving a specific root cause.
limitations: The load used the same instance public endpoint; the original OMA workload used its VPC endpoint, so network path and request mix differ.
DB active=0 in samples does not mean no SQL executed; short statements can finish between 1-2 second samples.

Storage process-local pool maximum, pending acquisition queue, in-use resources, service CPU/event-loop state and original error SQLSTATE/stack were not exposed. Cannot conclude pool too small or slow SQL solely from HTTP544.
GET bursts were observed before query-class/age sampling was enabled. GET idle-in-transaction counts do not establish transaction duration or where the GET path stopped.
Shared instance global totals include unrelated workloads. Classification counts are snapshot presences/peaks, not distinct requests.

The read-only test application role lacked visibility into other roles; its exploratory baseline is excluded. Production business data, SQL text/parameters, HTTP bodies and credentials are not in this summary.
